attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition captures the 'ultimately means' part but leaves out the hyperbolic 'refers to literally anything'. It is a reductive, characterising observation with a strong rhetorical tone.

contract.note: The plain reading (a conversational LM connected to systems, applied to current commercial agents) is ordinary and fair. Whether a model running in an adaptive tool loop counts as a 'chatbot' decides the result, and the speaker did not say.

evidence.note: A dated Anthropic demonstration within Q1 2026. It shows Claude sessions running in a loop with tools and shared state. It is consistent with the shorthand but is one vendor's prototype and cannot establish what the whole category means.

A dated Jan 2026 company disclosure describing multi-turn tool use and state changes. It qualifies the shorthand without clearly refuting it. It is a company statement about its own field, not an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only one vendor's materials. They show LLMs connected to tools in loops, which fits the components of Zitron's description. They neither establish nor refute that this adequately describes the whole agent category. The result depends on whether 'chatbot' covers looped, stateful LM execution, and the representative coverage the contract requires is missing.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, describing OpenClaw and Perplexity Computer.

semantics.note: The proposition widens the claim to 'agent products' in general, but the statement refers to the products just discussed (OpenClaw, Perplexity Computer). The square-peg framing is rhetorical.

contract.note: The contract fairly narrows the scope to the named products and reads 'compute-intensive' and 'hallucination-prone' in an ordinary way. The speaker gave no baseline or frequency, so the evaluator's thresholds decide the result.

evidence.note: OpenClaw's own versioned docs (Mar 31, 2026) describe a loop of model inference plus tool execution. This supports the 'LLM doing work' part only.
OpenClaw docs show the prompt is rebuilt each run and context keeps growing. This explains extra inference inputs but contains no measurement of compute intensity.
Perplexity's Feb 27, 2026 release says Opus 4.6 orchestrates 19 models. This supports LLM-driven orchestration but gives no compute or error data. It is a company disclosure.

A Feb 2026 preprint documents agents falsely reporting tasks as complete, in a setting the packet identifies as OpenClaw. This supports the hallucination component for OpenClaw only. The study is exploratory and partly adversarial, so it gives no prevalence.

reviews.rationale: Evidence establishes LLM-driven action for both products and false completion reports for OpenClaw. It has no compute measurements for either product and no hallucination evaluation for Perplexity Computer, both of which the support condition requires. Nothing contradicts the claim. The evidence available does not settle it as a whole.

attribution.note: Zitron states the figure in his own voice. The figure apparently comes from Bank of America Institute, but he presents it without qualification as his own assertion.

semantics.note: The proposition is faithful. 'Despite easy access' is framing, not a measurable condition.

contract.note: Reading unqualified 'households' as households in general, not one bank's customers, is the ordinary reading. The speaker did not name the population, so the result depends on which population and payment basis are used.

evidence.note: An independent BofA Institute measurement (Feb 2026 data, published Mar 30) finds about 3%, but only for Bank of America households paying through identified card or ACH channels. Representativeness for the general population is not shown.

A Feb 18, 2026 Parks release reports 16% of US internet households using a paid AI app. That counts use, not direct household payment, so it is not a comparable measure, and the fieldwork window is unclear.

reviews.rationale: The 3% figure matches BofA's measure for its own customers through its own payment channels, which is not a representative measure for households generally. Parks' 16% measures use of paid products rather than payment, so it does not contradict the claim on a comparable basis. Neither source settles the general-household share.
